title: (Scenario) A deployment suddenly increases API latency — how do you identify the root cause by comparing BEFORE vs AFTER the release (application metrics, distributed traces, DB performance, CPU/memory, GC activity, external dependencies, config changes, logs), and once the deploy is confirmed as the cause, how do you restore service safely using the org's rollback/deployment strategy?
shortTitle: Identifying a deploy as the cause of a latency spike by comparing BEFORE vs AFTER, then restoring service safely

s1_definition.profdef: You diagnose a post-deploy latency regression by comparing every relevant signal across the release boundary — application latency percentiles, distributed traces, database query performance, CPU and memory, garbage-collection activity, external dependency latency, configuration and feature-flag changes, and error logs — looking at the same metric just before and just after the deploy. If the signals change exactly at the deploy timestamp and only for the new version, the deploy is confirmed as the cause, and you restore service safely using the organization's rollback strategy, usually by rolling back to the last known-good version or flipping traffic away from the bad version.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine the National Bank of India's transfer service suddenly serves customers slowly right after a new process was rolled out. You line up yesterday's performance against today's, metric by metric — how long each transfer took, which step in the journey got slow, whether the ledger database is struggling, whether the servers are overloaded, whether the memory cleanup is thrashing, whether an outside partner got slow, and whether someone changed a setting. If everything looks normal except the numbers jumped exactly when the new process went live and only on the new counters, you have your culprit, and you simply switch customers back to the old process while you investigate.
s1_definition.oneliner: Compare every signal before and after the deploy at the exact release timestamp — if latency jumped only on the new version right at that moment, the deploy is the cause, and rolling back to the last known-good version is the fastest safe restore.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** You diagnose a post-deploy latency regression by comparing every relevant signal across the release boundary — application latency percentiles, distributed traces, database query performance, CPU and memory, garbage-collection activity, external dependency latency, configuration and feature-flag changes, and error logs — looking at the same metric just before and just after the deploy. If the signals change exactly at the deploy timestamp and only for the new version, the deploy is confirmed as the cause, and you restore service safely using the organization's rollback strategy, usually by rolling back to the last known-good version or flipping traffic away from the bad version.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine the National Bank of India's transfer service suddenly serves customers slowly right after a new process was rolled out. You line up yesterday's performance against today's, metric by metric — how long each transfer took, which step in the journey got slow, whether the ledger database is struggling, whether the servers are overloaded, whether the memory cleanup is thrashing, whether an outside partner got slow, and whether someone changed a setting. If everything looks normal except the numbers jumped exactly when the new process went live and only on the new counters, you have your culprit, and you simply switch customers back to the old process while you investigate.

**One line to remember:** Compare every signal before and after the deploy at the exact release timestamp — if latency jumped only on the new version right at that moment, the deploy is the cause, and rolling back to the last known-good version is the fastest safe restore.

sections.s2_technical:
The first move is to pin the deploy timestamp and overlay it on every dashboard, because the whole method is a before-and-after comparison anchored on that moment. You start with application metrics: look at p50, p95, and p99 latency and error rate for the endpoint, and check whether the jump coincides with the deploy and whether it affects only Pods or instances running the new version. If old-version instances stay fast and new-version instances are slow, that strongly implicates the release rather than external load.

Next you use distributed traces to find which span got slower. A trace shows the full journey of one request across services, so you compare a slow trace after the deploy with a fast trace before it and see exactly which hop grew — the database call, an external dependency, or internal computation. This narrows a vague "the API is slow" into "the account-lookup span went from 10 milliseconds to 400 milliseconds."

Then you check database performance, because a common regression is a new or changed query that lost an index or started doing a full table scan. You look at slow-query logs, query execution plans, lock waits, and connection-pool saturation, comparing query timings before and after. You also check CPU and memory on the instances, because a release can increase CPU through a hot loop or raise memory so high that the process is paging or being OOM-killed. Closely related is garbage-collection activity: a new version that allocates far more objects causes frequent or long GC pauses, which inflate tail latency, so you compare GC frequency and pause times across the boundary — a sudden rise in GC pause time right at the deploy is a classic cause of a p99 spike.

You also check external dependencies, because the slowdown might be a coincidence: a payment gateway or credit bureau got slow at the same time, and your deploy is innocent. Comparing external call latency rules this in or out. You review configuration and feature-flag changes, since the release may have shipped a config change — a smaller thread pool, a disabled cache, a new flag that enables an expensive code path — that is the real cause rather than the code itself. Finally you read error and warning logs filtered to the new version for timeouts, retries, and exceptions that appeared only after the deploy. When the evidence lines up — the regression starts exactly at the deploy, affects only the new version, and a specific span, query, or GC pattern changed — the deploy is confirmed as the cause.

Restoring service safely then follows the organization's rollback and deployment strategy. The fastest safe action is almost always to roll back to the last known-good version: with blue-green you flip traffic back to the stable environment instantly; with a rolling deployment you redeploy the previous image or run a rollout undo; with Kubernetes you use rollout undo to the prior ReplicaSet. If the cause was a feature flag or config, you flip the flag off or revert the config without a full rollback, which is even faster. Throughout, you keep stakeholders informed, you verify after rollback that latency returned to the pre-deploy baseline, and only once service is restored do you begin the deeper root-cause analysis and plan a safe re-release, typically behind a canary so the same regression would be caught at a small percentage next time.
sections.s3_banking:
The National Bank of India transfer API gets slow right after release v5.0. We want a comparator that takes before-deploy and after-deploy readings for each signal, flags which signals regressed, decides whether the deploy is the cause, and recommends the safe rollback action.

Problem 1 — "The API is slow" is not actionable. We must compare each signal across the deploy boundary to find which ones actually changed. This is exactly what a signal-by-signal before-and-after comparator does.

Problem 2 — Some regressions are coincidences (an external dependency got slow on its own). We must distinguish signals that the deploy controls from external ones, so we do not roll back for nothing.

Problem 3 — Once the deploy is confirmed, we need a clear safe restore action matching the deployment strategy. Our runnable Java simulation models a `SignalReading` (before and after values), a `RegressionAnalyzer` that computes percentage change and flags regressions, and a `RollbackAdvisor` that decides the restore action. Classes: `SignalReading`, `RegressionFinding`, `RegressionAnalyzer`, `RollbackAdvisor`, and a `DeployLatencyDemo` main.

sections.s4e_build:
```bash
# Build
mvn clean package -DskipTests

# Run the before/after latency analysis demo
java -cp target/classes com.bank.deploy.DeployLatencyDemo

# Real investigation commands
# overlay deploy marker on Grafana; compare p99 before/after
kubectl rollout history deployment/transfer-service
kubectl logs deploy/transfer-service --since=15m | grep -i 'timeout\|slow query'
# safe restore
kubectl rollout undo deployment/transfer-service
```
sections.s5_journey:
Input: a set of before-and-after readings taken at the v5.0 deploy boundary at 02:10:00.

Step 1 — The analyzer walks each signal and computes the percentage change from before to after. The p99 latency went from 120 to 650 milliseconds, a 442 percent rise, so it is flagged as regressed and deploy-controlled.

Step 2 — The account-lookup query went from 10 to 410 milliseconds, a 4000 percent rise, flagged as regressed and deploy-controlled — this is the smoking gun, a query that lost its index in the new version.

Step 3 — GC pause time rose from 80 to 520 milliseconds per minute, also regressed and deploy-controlled, explaining part of the tail-latency spike through longer pauses.

Step 4 — The payment gateway barely changed from 90 to 95 milliseconds and is marked external, so even if it had risen it would not justify a rollback; CPU and the thread-pool config are within the threshold.

Step 5 — Because at least one deploy-controlled signal regressed, the analyzer concludes the deploy is the cause. The advisor sees the regressions are code and query related, not config-only, so it recommends rolling back to the last known-good version, verifying p99 returns to baseline, and re-releasing behind a canary.

Final output:


sections.s6_takeaway:
When a deployment suddenly increases API latency, I diagnose it as a disciplined before-and-after comparison anchored on the exact deploy timestamp, which I overlay on every dashboard. I start with application metrics — p50, p95, and p99 latency and error rate — and I check whether the jump coincides with the deploy and affects only instances running the new version, because if the old version stays fast the release is implicated rather than external load. Then I use distributed traces to find which span got slower, comparing a slow trace after the deploy with a fast one before it, which turns "the API is slow" into "the account-lookup span went from ten to four hundred milliseconds."

From there I check database performance for a query that lost an index or started scanning, I check CPU and memory for a hot loop or memory pressure, and I pay special attention to garbage-collection activity, because a version that allocates far more objects causes longer or more frequent GC pauses that inflate tail latency, and a sudden rise in GC pause time right at the deploy is a classic p99 regression. I also compare external dependency latency so I do not blame my deploy for a payment gateway that got slow on its own, and I review configuration and feature-flag changes, since a smaller thread pool or a newly enabled expensive path can be the real cause. When the evidence lines up — the regression starts exactly at the deploy, affects only the new version, and a specific span, query, or GC pattern changed — I confirm the deploy as the cause.

To restore service safely I follow the organization's rollback strategy, and the fastest safe action is almost always to roll back to the last known-good version: a blue-green flip back to the stable environment, or a rollout undo to the previous ReplicaSet in Kubernetes. If the cause was a feature flag or config change, flipping the flag off or reverting the config is even faster than a full rollback. In my project at the National Bank of India, when transfer-service v5.0 spiked p99 latency for transfers involving Rajesh and Priya, this exact method showed the account-lookup query had lost its index and GC pauses had jumped, both only on the new version, so I rolled back immediately, verified p99 returned to its baseline, and then re-released behind a canary with automatic rollback. The principle I always state is mitigate first by rolling back, keep communicating, verify the baseline is restored, and only then do the deep root-cause analysis and a safe re-release.
